preamble: Total assimilation of the coda tap [ɾ] to a following [s], giving a voiceless geminate [ss]. In western Cuban Spanish (the provinces from Pinar del Río to Matanzas and Cienfuegos, including Havana, plus the municipalities of Corralillo and Trinidad), coda /ɾ/ and coda /l/ merge and assimilate to the next consonant. Before /s/ the assimilation is usually not total: several authors give [ds] (Ruiz Hernández 1974, Costa Sánchez 1984, Choy López, Dohotaru, Montero Bernal), and Arias (2019) calls [d˺s] the most usual pronunciation (farsa fa[ds]a, filed under ɾ > d). Goodgall de Pruna (1970) reports a voiceless [ss] in Trinidad, and Guitart (1978, 2004) describes [ss] (all as summarized by Arias 2019). Arias himself says that the tap is assimilated as a continuant before [s] "en la realización [ss]", beside the more usual [d˺s]. Arias (2019) writes these sequences as Guitart transcribes them across word boundaries, but notes that the realization is the same within words, where he writes [ds]; the transcriptions differ only because they follow different descriptions, not because the pronunciations differ. The unassimilated pronunciations remain more common.
phoneticEffects: Total Assimilation, Regressive Assimilation, Gemination, Devoicing

examples.note: Across a word boundary; Arias, following Guitart's description, glosses the form as 'mal salada o mar salada', because coda /l/ gives the same result. The sources consulted give only this one example.

sources: Arias Cabal, Á. (2019). Fonética y fonología de las consonantes geminadas en el español de Cuba. Moenia, 25, 465–497. https://revistas.usc.gal/index.php/moenia/article/view/6474
